title: HAWC maps TeV gamma rays beside the S106 star nursery
freshness: Unreviewed preprint submitted to arXiv on October 30, 2026; selected within the preferred 15-day window.
excerpt: HAWC has independently detected and mapped a very-high-energy gamma-ray source beside the S106 star-forming region. Fermi and Chandra data reveal lower-energy emission nearby, but the particles producing the TeV glow remain uncertain.
whyItMatters: Young stars, winds, jets, and dense molecular gas may turn star-forming regions into natural particle accelerators. Mapping the emission across X-ray and gamma-ray energies helps astronomers test whether electrons alone can power the glow or whether near-PeV protons also contribute.

body:
## A star nursery beside an extreme gamma-ray source

The High-Altitude Water Cherenkov Observatory, or HAWC, has detected a source of trillion-electronvolt gamma rays beside Sharpless 106, a region where stars are forming about 1,400 parsecs from Earth. One teraelectronvolt, abbreviated TeV, is a trillion electronvolts. That is far beyond the energy of visible light and points to particles accelerated in an extreme environment.

The source, 1LHAASO J2027+3657, had already appeared in a catalogue from the LHAASO observatory. The new HAWC analysis independently detected it above the team's five-sigma threshold and measured its shape and spectrum in greater detail. A five-sigma result is unlikely to arise from a random fluctuation under the assumptions of the analysis. HAWC's map preferred a spatial pattern based on dust measured by Planck over a simple point source. The same search also uncovered a separate, still-unidentified TeV point source named HAWC J2018+3610 elsewhere in the field.

S106 is a bipolar cloud shaped by a central young binary and surrounded by other young stars. It lies close to J2027 on the sky, but the TeV emission is offset from the nursery itself. That makes their physical relationship plausible, not proven.

## Three observatories, one energy spectrum

The researchers reanalysed Fermi Large Area Telescope data collected between August 2008 and July 2024. They found extended gamma-ray emission from 200 megaelectronvolts to 1 TeV near S106 at about 11-sigma significance. They also revisited a roughly 45-kilosecond Chandra observation. After masking known point sources, they measured diffuse X-ray emission that accounts for about 10 percent of S106's total X-ray luminosity. Some unresolved stars could remain in that diffuse component.

Putting the X-ray and gamma-ray measurements together creates a broad energy spectrum. The team tested whether one population of energetic electrons could explain it. In that model, lower-energy electrons produce gamma rays while passing through dense gas, and higher-energy electrons boost S106's abundant infrared photons to TeV energies through inverse Compton scattering. That term describes a fast electron transferring energy to a low-energy photon. Including the nursery's local infrared field lets the electron-only model reproduce the observed spectrum.

An alternative model also works. It allows energetic protons to collide with matter and create particles that decay into gamma rays. In this fit, the proton cutoff reaches the model's upper boundary of 1,000 TeV, or 1 PeV. That makes the region a possible PeVatron, an accelerator capable of pushing particles toward petaelectronvolt energies, but it is not a measured proton cutoff or proof that S106 is a PeVatron.

## What is measured and what remains open

**Measured:** HAWC detected and spatially modelled J2027; Fermi found extended GeV emission near S106; Chandra recorded a diffuse X-ray component after known point sources were removed.

**Inferred:** Winds or jets from the young stellar system may accelerate the particles, and S106's infrared light may help electrons generate the TeV glow. A substantial proton contribution remains possible because both model families fit the broadband data.

The paper is an unreviewed preprint, so its conclusions are preliminary. Its clearest result is the multiwavelength map itself: a star-forming complex and a nearby TeV source now have a connected set of measurements, while the identity and transport of the fastest particles remain unsettled.
